clue.text: "Who are those hooded — swarming / Over endless plains" (T. S. Eliot)

definitions.text: "Who are those hooded — swarming / Over endless plains" (T. S. Eliot)

parts.words: "Who are those hooded — swarming / Over endless plains" (T. S. Eliot)
parts.note: a line from part V of The Waste Land with one word left out; the solver supplies the missing noun for the swarming crowds

explanation.surface: A quotation from Eliot's The Waste Land with a gap where one word should be.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank: the missing word from Eliot's line is the answer, and it fits the sense of swarming multitudes.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap stands for a word meaning vast swarming crowds, which is what Eliot's line describes.

clue.text: Can I have your attention about Guy Alharthi, perhaps

indicators.note: about means one piece goes around the other here

parts.note: OI is the British shout used to get someone's attention
a guy is a man

explanation.surface: Someone calls for attention to talk about a person called Guy Alharthi.
explanation.walkthrough: Jokha Alharthi is the novelist from Oman who won the International Booker for Celestial Bodies; 'perhaps' marks her as an example, and 'about' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Jokha Alharthi is a novelist from Oman, so she is an example of someone of that nationality.

clue.text: Poet that has held past service for chap who knocked out O'Malley of Shanganagh

definitions.text: chap who knocked out O'Malley of Shanganagh

indicators.note: has held means the poet's name contains the other letters

parts.note: John Donne, the metaphysical poet
by can mean past, as in walking by
RN is the Royal Navy, a fighting service

explanation.surface: A poet, once in the services, is replaced by someone who beat an Irishman in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Donn Byrne was an Irish-American writer whose novella O'Malley of Shanganagh appeared in 1925; 'knocked out' means wrote quickly, not floored in a boxing ring.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish-American author Donn Byrne wrote, or dashed off, the short novel O'Malley of Shanganagh.

clue.text: Detective one's seen out in front of a factory briefly

indicators.note: briefly tells us to drop the final letter of the word

parts.words: one's seen out in front of a factory
parts.note: a worker who has walked out is seen picketing at the factory gates

explanation.surface: A detective spots someone standing outside a factory for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts the last letter from STRIKER. Cormoran Strike is the private detective in the novels Robert Galbraith (J. K. Rowling) writes.
explanation.definitionFit: Cormoran Strike is the private investigator who heads Robert Galbraith's crime series.

clue.text: Fine city house finally demolished by a Joad's birthplace

parts.note: OK means fine or all right
LA is Los Angeles

indicators.note: the last letter of the word for house is knocked away

parts.note: a home is a house

explanation.surface: A fine house in a city is pulled down, at the place where a Joad was born.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally demolished' removes the E from HOME. The Joads are the dust-bowl family who leave home and head west in Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's Joad family are Dust Bowl farmers who leave this state for California.

clue.text: A famous novel, one we are all familiar with?

definitions.text: one we are all familiar with?
definitions.meaning: taken literally, a pal shared by all of us

explanation.surface: A celebrated novel is one everybody knows.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the Dickens title literally as a companion everybody shares; the question mark flags that playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's last completed novel takes its title from a phrase meaning a friend shared by speaker and listener.

clue.text: Naughty cleaner grabs Welsh writer renowned for sex

indicators.note: grabs means the jumbled word takes hold of a letter inside it
naughty suggests the letters of the following word behave badly and get mixed up

explanation.surface: A badly behaved cleaner seizes a Welsh author known for racy books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naughty' scrambles CLEANER, and 'grabs' puts W inside. The author is D. H. Lawrence, of Lady Chatterley's Lover; the Welsh writer the surface suggests is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence was notorious for frank sexual content, above all in Lady Chatterley's Lover.

clue.text: Try to get piece from Nara for Japanese ghost story publisher

parts.note: to hear a case is to try it in court

indicators.note: a piece from the city's name here is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone tries to buy a bit from Nara for a publisher of Japanese ghost stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Lafcadio Hearn collected and published Japanese ghost stories in Kwaidan (1904).
explanation.definitionFit: Lafcadio Hearn published Kwaidan, a well-known collection of Japanese supernatural tales.

clue.text: Diamond one of The Who's given to Brian Jones?

parts.note: Keith Moon was The Who's drummer
Brian Jones was a founding member of the Rolling Stones

explanation.surface: A diamond belonging to a member of The Who is handed to Brian Jones.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces come from 1960s rock: Keith Moon of The Who and Brian Jones of the Rolling Stones. The definition is the cursed Indian gem in Wilkie Collins's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilkie Collins's novel centres on a stolen Indian diamond of that name.

clue.text: Shrewd series about Queen work featuring a riotous party

indicators.note: about means the word for shrewd goes around the royal abbreviation

parts.note: canny means shrewd
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen
a row is a series or line

explanation.surface: A shrewd sequence about the Queen's work that includes a wild party.
explanation.walkthrough: Steinbeck's novel famously has a party for Doc that gets out of hand and wrecks his laboratory; 'about' wraps the Queen in the shrewd word, not in the series.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's novel about Monterey drifters includes a well-meant party for Doc that ends in chaos.

clue.text: Religious book Money author makes Self start to open

indicators.note: makes signals that one letter is turned into another

parts.note: Martin Amis wrote the novel Money
I is the self, the speaker

indicators.note: the start of the word open is its opening letter

explanation.surface: The author of Money turns Will Self into a writer of religious books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' changes the I in AMIS to O, the start of 'open'. The surface teases with Will Self, another novelist, but 'Self' is just I.
explanation.definitionFit: Amos is a book of the Old Testament, named after the prophet.

clue.text: Work involving the homeless in a foreign capital

definitions.meaning: Paul Auster's 1999 novel follows a homeless man and his dog
a West African city, historic capital of learning and of its region of Mali

explanation.surface: A job helping homeless people in a city abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Auster's novel is about the homeless Willy G. Christmas and his dog Mr Bones; the same name belongs to the city in Mali, capital of its region.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Auster's novel about a vagrant and his dog shares its title with the Malian city.

clue.text: Papa was one serious in mind, according to hearsay

indicators.note: hearsay signals the word is heard, not seen, giving a similar-sounding name

parts.note: earnest means serious and sincere

explanation.surface: Father was a solemn sort, or so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papa' was Ernest Hemingway's nickname, so the definition is a first name; the sound-alike is Wilde's punning title in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Hemingway, nicknamed Papa, had this first name.

clue.text: One interrupting flipping odd linesman

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking into the other word
flipping turns the word for odd backwards

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone butts in on a strange football linesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' turns RUM into MUR, and 'interrupting' puts I into it. A 'linesman' here is a poet, a writer of lines: Edwin Muir, the Orkney poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin Muir was a Scottish poet, so a writer of lines of verse.

clue.text: "Seen birds of tempest-loving kind / Thus beating — the wind" (Wordsworth)

definitions.text: "Seen birds of tempest-loving kind / Thus beating — the wind" (Wordsworth)

parts.words: "Seen birds of tempest-loving kind / Thus beating — the wind" (Wordsworth)
parts.note: Wordsworth lines with a two-word gap; the solver supplies the phrase for birds flying into the gale

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth with a gap where two words should be.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank: the missing phrase completes Wordsworth's picture of storm birds beating into a headwind.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a phrase meaning facing or opposing, as birds fly straight into the wind.

clue.text: Servile character in The Pawnbroker needing brass

parts.note: uncle is old British slang for a pawnbroker
brass and tom are both British slang for a prostitute

explanation.surface: In the film The Pawnbroker, a character needs money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brass' looks like money, but it is slang for a prostitute (from rhyming slang brass nail), as is tom. The character is from Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The title figure of Stowe's novel became a byword for a submissive, subservient person.

clue.text: People like Karl Oskar's record label to get subsidies

parts.note: EMI is a British record company
grants are subsidies

explanation.surface: A record label belonging to someone called Karl Oskar gets funding.
explanation.walkthrough: Karl Oskar Nilsson leads the Swedish family that leaves for America in Vilhelm Moberg's novel series, the first part titled after such people.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Oskar leaves Sweden for Minnesota in Moberg's novels, so he is one who leaves his homeland to settle abroad.

clue.text: Name one associates with good man and old nymph

parts.note: to ... name
I is the Roman numeral one
ST, saint, is a good man

explanation.surface: A name people link with a good man and an ancient nymph.
explanation.walkthrough: Callisto was the nymph loved by Zeus and turned into a bear, then the Great Bear constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Callisto was a nymph of Artemis whom Zeus seduced.

clue.text: Bud Parusha's game for a debauched dance, perhaps

parts.note: base means low and immoral
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A character's sport offered in place of a dissolute dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Bud Parusha is the one-armed outfielder of the hapless Ruppert Mundys in Philip Roth's The Great American Novel, so his game is America's national pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: The character Bud Parusha plays the American bat-and-ball sport.

clue.text: Playwright who adapted The Liar's head came out in rash!

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word goes missing

parts.note: hives is an itchy skin rash

explanation.surface: A playwright breaks out in a rash, starting from his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head came out' removes H from HIVES. David Ives adapted Corneille's comedy The Liar in 2010.
explanation.definitionFit: The American dramatist David Ives wrote a verse adaptation of Corneille's The Liar.

clue.text: When actor will put up cold Elizabethan writer

indicators.note: put up means give lodging, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he left'
a ham is an overacting actor
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: An actor will lodge someone feeling the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will put up' means give lodging to. Roger Ascham was tutor to the young Elizabeth I and wrote The Scholemaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Ascham was a scholar and author at the court of Elizabeth I.

clue.text: Potential lunch for old hag ashen criminal left

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are crooked and rearranged

explanation.surface: A pale crook leaves the witch's prospective meal behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges ASHEN. In the Grimms' tale the witch fattens Hansel to eat him.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fairy tale the witch plans to cook and eat the boy, so he is a meal in waiting.

clue.text: Small policeman arresting Oscar in a tale of mistaken identity

indicators.note: arresting means holding the letter inside

parts.note: a cop is a policeman
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A short policeman arrests a man named Oscar who turns out to be the wrong person.
explanation.walkthrough: Evelyn Waugh's Scoop sends the nature writer William Boot to cover a war by mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Waugh's satire hinges on the wrong Boot being sent abroad as a war correspondent.

clue.text: Answer given by Pope concerning playwright's output?

parts.note: re means concerning
a playwright writes a script

explanation.surface: The Pope replies about a dramatist's work.
explanation.walkthrough: A papal rescript is the Pope's written reply to a query or petition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rescript is a formal written reply from a pope or emperor.

clue.text: Commoner with duty to accompany prince

indicators.note: to accompany means the duty word goes along beside the prince's letter

parts.note: a role is a duty or function

explanation.surface: An ordinary person's job is to escort a prince.
explanation.definitionFit: A prole, from Orwell's 1984, is a member of the working class.

clue.text: One Japanese drama filled with bit of freebasing and dope

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: filled with means the drama's name holds a letter inside

parts.note: Noh, also spelt No, is classical Japanese theatre

indicators.note: a bit of the word here is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone at a Japanese play is full of freebased drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'filled with' puts F inside NO. 'dope' is slang for information, not drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Dope is slang for inside information or the lowdown.

clue.text: Famous Scottish writer put on the radio for Rocket Man

indicators.note: on the radio means as broadcast and heard, so a similar-sounding name

parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island

explanation.surface: A celebrated Scottish author is broadcast as Elton John's song.
explanation.walkthrough: George Stephenson built the Rocket locomotive in 1829; 'Rocket Man' sounds like the Elton John song.
explanation.definitionFit: George Stephenson's engine the Rocket won the Rainhill Trials, so he is the man behind it.

clue.text: Car mogul seen on stage in robot-manufacturing town

indicators.note: seen on means placed after, standing on the stage

parts.note: a step is a stage
Henry Ford was the car magnate

explanation.surface: A motor magnate is spotted on stage in a town that makes robots.
explanation.walkthrough: In Ira Levin's The Stepford Wives the town's men replace their wives with robots.
explanation.definitionFit: In Ira Levin's novel the Connecticut town's husbands secretly turn their wives into compliant automata.

clue.text: Successful chess player holding son for Henry James?

indicators.note: holding means the player word contains the letter

parts.note: one who mates the opponent's king

explanation.surface: A winning chess player hangs on to his son for the novelist Henry James.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts S inside MATER. Colm Tóibín's novel about Henry James is titled The Master, and James was so called; the question mark marks the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Colm Tóibín's novel about Henry James calls him by this title, given to a revered artist.
